newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left issues plan, claims boost from Blair.
newsitem.headline: French left issues plan, claims boost from Blair.

text.p: France's opposition Socialists on Friday issued their election manifesto pledging to create jobs and cut the working week as both the left and the right claimed a boost from the Labour Party's big win in Britain.

The Socialists, in the second week of campaigning in a snap two-round parliamentary election called by conservative President Jacques Chirac for May 25 and June 1, sought to draw a sharp contrast with the ruling centre-right coalition.

"Let's change economic and social policies, let's change the everyday life of the French, let's change Europe, let's change our democracy," Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin told party members to rousing cheers.
In a bizarre sidelight to the campaign, Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy was slashed by a knife-wielding assailant while campaigning in the southwestern city of Lourdes.

Douste-Blazy was rushed to hospital but his injury, a knife cut in the back, was not life-threatening. A "mentally unstable" Albanian man who was captured shortly after the attack was being held by police.
On the day after the Labour landslide in Britain, France's left and right tried to claim as their ideological soul mate labour's triumphant leader Tony Blair.

"It is the friends of Mr (French Prime Minister Alain) Juppe and Mr Chirac who just got beat in Great Britain and it is the friends of the French Socialists who just brought off a victory," Jospin said in unveiling his party's manifesto.
On the right, leaders said Labour won the election because it "was smart enough to throw into the Thames certain outmoded precepts" about state control of the economy.

Chirac congratulated Blair for his "outstanding success" and invited the new British premier to visit Paris while Juppe said it was "liberal Labour that won because Blair modernised his party and rejected Socialism".

Though offering support for a single European currency, the Socialists attached conditions, including a flexible interpretation of Maastricht treaty criteria and membership for all who wanted it including Spain, Italy and Britain.

They also said they wanted a European economic government alongside the future European central bank and that the party would review a stability pact meant to limit budget deficits after the launch of the new euro.

The Socialists' platform proposed reforms in payroll charges to cut the cost of labour, state-backed schemes to create 700,000 jobs, and a cut in the work week to 35 hours from 39 without loss of pay.

The party, lagging in opinion polls, also promised to make education the top budget priority, force the wealthy to pay more taxes and repeal controversial laws, passed under conservative governments, which tightened controls on immigration.
They vowed to maintain public services in security, education, transport, health, post and telecoms.
"We reject privatisation of public services and turning them into groups devoted to profit," the manifesto said.
The party said the 700,000 jobs would be paid for without raising public spending by scrapping other job creation schemes.

Unemployment and Europe are the top issues in the French campaign with tight limits on public spending to help Paris qualify for European monetary union and unemployment at a record 12.8 percent of the workforce.
Criticism of the plan from the centre-right coalition was swift and sharp, with Juppe saying he was "staggered" by what he said were expensive promises.

"Who would pay? Obviously the taxpayer, and this would mean an inescapable rise in taxes," Juppe said while campaigning in Bordeaux in the southwest. "This is really a programme that would be harmful for our country."
